relevance_reason: Discovery paper that identifies de novo heterozygous variants in the 18-bp critical region of RNU4-2 as the cause of this syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. It includes clinical characterization, the variant spectrum, parent-of-origin data, splicing (RNA-seq) studies and prevalence estimates.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) identified the noncoding RNA gene RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 snRNA of the major spliceosome U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP, as a gene for an autosomal dominant syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. They found heterozygous variants in 115 individuals with NDD, all within an 18-bp region of RNU4-2 that maps to the T-loop and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex and is severely depleted of variation in the general population.
quotes: We identify an 18 base pair region of RNU4-2 mapping to two structural elements in the U4/U6 snRNA duplex (the T-loop and stem III) that is severely depleted of variation in the general population, but in which we identify heterozygous variants in 115 individuals with NDD.
Here we identify variants in RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 snRNA component of the major spliceosome, in an autosomal dominant disorder.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) identified a highly recurrent single-base insertion in RNU4-2 (n.64_65insT; GRCh38 chr12:120291839:T:TA) in the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project. It arose de novo in 38 probands sequenced with both unaffected parents, and 8 more individuals had findings consistent with de novo occurrence. All 46 had undiagnosed NDD, which was 0.52% of 8,841 undiagnosed NDD probands. The variant was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0 and All of Us, and was seen in only 1 individual in UK Biobank. Across all cohorts, 89 of the 115 affected individuals (77.4%) carried this variant.
quotes: We identified a highly recurrent single base insertion (GRCh38:chr. 12: 120291839:T:TA; n.64_65insT) in RNU4-2 in GEL. This variant was initially identified as arising de novo in 38 probands recruited for genome sequencing with their unaffected parents.
The n.64_65insT variant was not found in any of 3,408 NDD probands with an existing genetic diagnosis, 21,817 probands with non-NDD phenotypes or 33,122 unaffected individuals.
Most of the 115 individuals have the initial n.64_65insT variant (n = 89; 77.4%).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) reported a second recurrent single-base insertion in RNU4-2, n.77_78insT (GRCh38 chr12:120291826:T:TA), in 6 individuals, including 2 affected sibs. In total, 6 different single-base insertions in the critical region were found in 100 individuals. Single-base insertions in this region were present in 54 of 8,841 undiagnosed GEL NDD probands, compared with 2 of 490,132 UK Biobank individuals (OR = 1,531).
quotes: Five of the 11 extra variants are also single base insertions, including n.77_78insT (GRCh38:chr. 12: 120291826:T:TA), which is seen in six individuals, two of whom are affected siblings.

54 out of 8,841 (0.61%) GEL undiagnosed NDD probands (55 out of 10,388 individuals) have single base insertions compared to two out of 490,132 individuals in the UK Biobank (OR = 1,531; 95% confidence interval (CI): 404–16,384; Fisher’s P = 3.3 × 10−92).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) identified 15 individuals with SNVs in the RNU4-2 critical region; 10 were confirmed de novo, and all had phenotypes consistent with those of individuals with insertions. The SNVs clustered at both ends of the 18-bp region. SNVs were modestly enriched in GEL NDD probands compared with UK Biobank (OR = 9.51). In 1 individual, the n.65A>G variant appeared to be mosaic in the mother, and in another the SNV n.76C>T was maternally inherited. SNVs at the center of the region (nucleotides 71-74) were also found in non-NDD individuals and population controls.
quotes: We identified 15 individuals across cohorts with SNVs in this region (Extended Data Table 1; 10 confirmed de novo), all with phenotypes consistent with individuals with insertion variants.
In one individual the n.65A>G variant appeared to be mosaic in the mother (54 reference and eight alternate reads) and in another an SNV was maternally inherited (n.76C>T).

Conversely, SNVs in the central portion (particularly at nucleotides 71–74) are observed in both non-NDD individuals in GEL (n = 2) and population controls, although all at low frequencies (Extended Data Table 1).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) noted that other single-base insertions in RNU4-2 included n.68_69insA and n.64_65insG, each found in individuals described clinically in the study.
quotes: All individuals shown have the n.64_65insT variant, except for individual 44 in o (n.68_69insA), individual 45 in p (n.64_65insG) and individual 48 in q (n.76C>T).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) confirmed de novo occurrence with parental sequencing in 86 of 115 individuals. In all 54 individuals in whom the parental allele of origin could be resolved, the variant was on the maternal allele, in contrast to the usual paternal bias for de novo mutations. The authors suggested this could reflect negative selection in the male germline or imprinting. No maternal age effect was seen.
quotes: For 86 of the 115 individuals, sequencing data for both parents were available to confirm that the variants had arisen de novo.
For 54 individuals in whom this could be confidently resolved (46 with n.64_65insT; three with other insertion variants; five with SNVs), all 54 were present on the maternal allele.

The absence of any paternally derived variants in our cohort may be a consequence of negative selection in the male germline if RNU4-2 plays an important role during spermatogenesis. It may also be a consequence of imprinting

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypes for 49 individuals (21 female, 28 male; median age 10 years, range 2-38). Of these, 42 had n.64_65insT, 3 had other insertions and 4 had SNVs. All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Most (83%) walked, but late (mean 3.4 years), some with a wide-based or ataxic gait. Most were nonverbal. Other common features were short stature (76%), microcephaly (77%, mostly congenital), hypotonia (87%), seizures (77%; median onset 3 years), abnormal brain MRI (91%), vision problems (79%), autism (48%), feeding difficulties and constipation.
quotes: Using these data, we find the RNU4-2 syndromic NDD to be characterized by moderate to severe global developmental delay (four children with SNVs with moderate delay) and intellectual disability in all individuals.

Most (83%) achieved ambulation but at a delayed age (average 3.4 years, range 17 months to 7.5 years) with some noted to have a wide-based or ataxic gait. Only three individuals (two with an SNV) had fluent speech, some had a few words and most were non-verbal.

Associated growth and neurodevelopmental phenotypes present in more than or equal to 75% of individuals include short stature, microcephaly (mostly congenital), speech abnormalities (mostly non-verbal), hypotonia and seizures.

phenotypes.onset: first year of life to 10 years

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) reported that 45 of 48 individuals had dysmorphic facial features. These varied, but included a myopathic face with deep-set eyes, epicanthus, a wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, large cupped ears, full cheeks, full lips with downturned corners, a high-arched palate and a large or protruding tongue.
quotes: These facial features varied but consisted of a myopathic face with deep set eyes (some widely spaced and some narrowly spaced), epicanthus, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped ala nasi, large cupped ears (some posteriorly rotated), full cheeks, a distinctive mouth with full lips with downturned corners, high arched palate and a large or protruding tongue (Fig. 3).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) reported that brain MRI showed abnormalities in most individuals, most often reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly and delayed myelination. Many organ systems were involved, including skeletal (osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, hip dysplasia), endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, pituitary abnormalities), visual (including cortical blindness), genitourinary, dental and cutaneous. Presentation did not differ significantly between males and females.
quotes: Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed a spectrum of abnormalities in most individuals, most frequently reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, delayed myelination and other non-specific abnormalities of the white matter.

bone and/or skeletal abnormalities (osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, hip dysplasia) and in fewer individuals, hearing, endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, pituitary abnormalities), limb, sleep, genitourinary, dental, cardiac and cutaneous concerns

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that, compared with all other NDD probands in GEL, individuals with the n.64_65insT variant were significantly enriched for HPO terms for global developmental delay, delayed gross and fine motor development, microcephaly, hypotonia, short stature, drooling and absent speech.
quotes: Individuals with the variant are significantly enriched for global developmental delay (n = 37; odds ratio (OR) = 3.56; Fisher’s P = 2.75 × 10−4), delayed gross motor development (n = 26; OR = 2.55; P = 1.64 × 10−3), microcephaly (n = 26; OR = 6.62; P = 7.87 × 10−10)
drooling (n = 7; OR = 19.2; P = 2.83 × 10−7) and absent speech (n = 6; OR = 6.23; P = 7.45 × 10−4)

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that children with SNVs had fewer reports of severe global developmental delay than those with single-base insertions (0 of 4 vs 34 of 40). Two of the 3 individuals with fluent speech had an SNV, and fewer organ systems were involved in those with SNVs. The authors suggested that SNVs may cause a milder phenotype, but noted that this needs confirmation in larger cohorts.
quotes: In comparison to the single base insertions, children with SNVs had fewer reports of severe global developmental delay (zero out of four versus 34 out of 40, Fisher’s P = 0.0015).

Although we do also observe some SNVs in this region in individuals with NDD, our initial data suggest these SNVs may result in a milder phenotype. However, given this observation is based on only four fully phenotyped individuals, it needs to be confirmed in larger cohorts.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) analyzed blood RNA-seq data from 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants (3 with n.64_65insT, 1 with n.77_78insT and 1 with n.78A>C). Compared with controls, these individuals showed significantly more abnormal splicing events at unannotated 5-prime splice sites (mean 8.8 vs 0.7). Splicing events shared by 2 or more patients were not found in any of 378 controls. At sites with increased use, positions +3 to +5, which pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence, shifted away from consensus. The authors concluded that the variants disrupt accurate 5-prime splice-site recognition during spliceosome activation.
quotes: Consistent with the importance of the critical region in 5′ splice-site recognition, the most pronounced difference was observed for abnormal splicing events corresponding to increased use of unannotated 5′ splice sites (mean 8.8 events in individuals with RNU4-2 variants compared with 0.7 in both 378 unmatched controls and ten controls matched on genetic ancestry, sex and age at consent

Of all the detected abnormal splicing events, 12 of these were shared by two or more individuals with RNU4-2 variants (Extended Data Table 3). Eleven of these 12 events (91.6%) corresponded to an increase in unannotated 5′ splice-site use. None of these shared events were identified in any of the 378 controls.

shift away from consensus at sites with increased use in individuals with RNU4-2 variants provides functional evidence that these variants disrupt accurate splice-site recognition during spliceosome activation.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region (nucleotides 62-79) is loaded into the active site of the BRR2 (SNRNP200) helicase. The n.64_65insT variant lies within a T-loop (quasi-pseudoknot), and n.77_78insT lies in the stem III region that pairs with U6. The authors proposed that single-base insertions destabilize the U4/U6 interaction and/or alter the positioning of the U6 ACAGAGA sequence that receives the 5-prime splice site.
quotes: This region is known to be loaded into the active site of the SNRNP200-encoded BRR2 helicase, which mediates spliceosome activation by unwinding the U4/U6 duplex. The highly recurrent n.64_65insT variant is within a previously described ‘quasi pseudoknot’, or T-loop, structure (Fig. 1d).

Specifically, insertion of a single base into the T-loop or stem III regions may destabilize the U4/U6 interaction and/or alter the positioning of the U6 ACAGAGA sequence and potentially disrupt the correct loading of the 5′ splice site into the fully assembled spliceosome.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found variants in the 18-bp RNU4-2 region in 60 of 8,841 (0.68%) genetically undiagnosed GEL NDD probands, compared with 39 of 490,132 (0.008%) UK Biobank individuals. Assuming a prior diagnostic yield of 40%, they estimated that RNU4-2 variants explain about 0.4% of all NDD. The rate was much lower in autism cohorts (3 of 7,149). The authors noted that the variant region is not captured by clinical exome sequencing.
quotes: This includes 60 out of 8,841, or 0.68%, of all genetically undiagnosed NDD probands in GEL. By contrast, variants in this region are observed in 39 out of 490,132 (0.008%) individuals in the UK Biobank
we estimate that variants in RNU4-2 could explain 0.4% of all NDD (calculated as 60 from an effective cohort size of 14,735 (8,841 × 1/0.6)).

This is consistent with the much lower rate of RNU4-2 variants in cohorts recruited primarily for autism spectrum disorder (for example, three out of 7,149; 0.042% across the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC), SPARK and MSSNG).

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that exome sequencing has very low sensitivity for detecting the n.64_65insT variant. Of 22 individuals with the variant who also had DDD exome data, only 2 had any read at the position, and in both cases the read showed the reference sequence. The authors stated that any variant found this way requires independent confirmation.
quotes: Of 1,755 individuals in both GEL and DDD, 22 have the n.64_65insT variant (1.3%). Two of the 22 individuals (9.1%) each have a single read at the variant position in the exome sequencing data from DDD, but in each case it is identical to the reference sequence.
These analyses suggest that although it is possible to identify individuals who may have variants in RNU4-2 through exome sequencing data, the sensitivity of this approach is very low.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that RNU4-2 and RNU4-1 are adjacent on chromosome 12, are both 141 bp long and differ at 4 nucleotides. RNU4-2 was expressed at consistently higher levels than RNU4-1 across development in human prefrontal cortex (BrainVar). Prenatal cortex ATAC-seq showed much greater chromatin accessibility at RNU4-2, supporting RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain. Variants in RNU4-1 were not enriched in NDD.
quotes: RNU4-2 and RNU4-1 are contiguous on chr. 12, both 141 bp long and highly homologous, differing by four nucleotides (97.2% similarity).
The expression of RNU4-1 and RNU4-2 is tightly correlated (Supplementary Fig. 5), however, RNU4-2 is consistently expressed at a significantly higher level than RNU4-1 (Fig. 5a).
Overall, these data support the role of RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2024) examined 28 other brain-expressed snRNA genes and found no other snRNA, or constrained subregion of one, significantly enriched for de novo or biallelic variants in undiagnosed NDD probands. RNU12 showed only nominal enrichment of biallelic variants.
quotes: We did not find any other snRNAs, or constrained subregions of snRNAs, that were significantly enriched for either de novo variants or recessively inherited variants in NDD cases when compared with non-NDD probands.
We observed a nominal enrichment of variants in RNU12 (11 probands with NDD versus two non-NDD probands; Fisher’s P = 0.026), but this was not significant after correcting for multiple testing.

relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with a de novo RNU4-2 variant causing ReNU syndrome, with clinical phenotype.

findings.statement: Schot et al. (2024) reported a 5-year-old girl with severe global developmental delay, hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures, followed over 5 years; photographs showed facial features the authors considered recognizable for this novel disorder.
quotes: in a 5-year-old girl with severe global developmental delay, hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures that likely explains her phenotype
This includes photographs showing recognizable facial features for this novel disorder

findings.statement: By mining 164 diagnostic WGS trios from individuals with neurodevelopmental or multiple congenital anomaly disorders, Schot et al. (2024) identified a recurrent de novo variant in the noncoding spliceosomal snRNA gene RNU4-2 (NR_003137.2:n.64_65insT) in the girl, whose earlier extensive genetic investigations had not identified an alternative cause. The authors concluded that the variant likely explained her phenotype.
quotes: Here we mined 164 whole genome sequencing (WGS) trios from individuals with neurodevelopmental or multiple congenital anomaly disorders that received diagnostic genomic investigations at our clinic.
We identify a recurrent de novo RNU4-2 variant (NR_003137.2(RNU4-2):n.64_65insT)
given that extensive previous genetic investigations failed to identify an alternative cause

relevance_reason: This is the discovery paper for de novo RNU4-2 variants causing ReNU syndrome. It covers the genetic association, the variants, replication, phenotype frequencies, prevalence and the proposed mechanism.

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) ran a genetic association analysis on whole-genome sequencing data from the 100,000 Genomes Project. They compared the burden of rare variants in 41,132 noncoding genes between 5,529 unrelated intellectual disability (ID) cases and 46,401 unrelated controls. They identified an extremely strong dominant association between rare variants in RNU4-2, which encodes U4 snRNA, and ID (posterior probability of association about 1, log Bayes factor 55). None of the 34 ID cases carrying the 3 top variants had previously received a diagnosis, and these cases were phenotypically more homogeneous than expected by chance.
quotes: We identified an extremely strong dominant association between rare variants in RNU4-2 and the risk of ID (posterior probability of association (PPA) ≈ 1, log Bayes factor = 55).

None of the 34 cases were previously solved through an explanatory pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variant, representing a significant depletion compared to the 20.1% of ID cases overall explained through the 100KGP diagnostic pipeline

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) found 8 rare variants in 2 contiguous regions of RNU4-2 (n.62-70 and n.73-79) that were present only in affected participants. These regions lie in a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Across 47 cases in the 100,000 Genomes Project, 37 variants were de novo and 10 had unknown inheritance. The variants were n.63T>G, n.64_65insG, n.64_65insT, n.65A>G, n.65_66insT, n.67A>G and n.68_69insA in the quasi-pseudoknot region, and n.76C>T and n.77_78insT in stem III.
quotes: Of the 47 rare allele instances in the regions, which we observed in 47 cases, 37 were determined to be de novo on the basis of genotype calls in the respective parents, while 10 had unknown inheritance because of missing genotypes from one or both of the corresponding parents

are predicted to disrupt Watson-Crick interactions within U4 stem III (n.76 C > T and n.77_78insT) or to disrupt configuration of the U4 quasi-pseudoknot (n.63 T > G; n.64_65insG; n.64_65insT; n65A>G; n.65_66insT; n.67 A > G and n.68_69insA)

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) reported that the most common RNU4-2 variant, n.64_65insT, arose as a de novo mutation in 33 different families. They noted that G64 of U4 snRNA is thought to help stabilize the ACAGAGA loop of U6 snRNA. They also proposed that the insertion could disrupt the G64(U4)-A47(U6) interaction that supports the quasi-pseudoknot.
quotes: The most common variant, n.64_65insT, was observed as a de novo mutation in 33 different families.
Given that the predominant variant, n.64_65insT, could disrupt the G64(U4)–A47(U6) interaction supporting the quasi-pseudoknot structure

findings.statement: In 100,000 Genomes Project pedigree G38, Greene et al. (2024) identified the RNU4-2 n.65A>G variant in a heterozygous male proband. His mother was called homozygous for the reference allele but was likely mosaic for the variant when the aligned WGS reads were inspected.
quotes: one of the parents was mosaic for n.65A>G, while the remainder had confident heterozygous or homozygous reference genotype calls
shows the read pileups at this position in the heterozygous proband of pedigree G38 and his mother, who had a homozygous reference genotype call but is likely mosaic

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) replicated their findings in 3 collections: the NIHR BioResource, the 100,000 Genomes Project Pilot and the UK Genomic Medicine Service. Together these contributed 27 further probands with a rare variant in the 2 RNU4-2 regions, of whom 26 were affected and 1 was unaffected. Of the 26 affected probands, 19 had a de novo variant, 6 had unknown inheritance, and 1 inherited n.76C>T from an affected mother. This brought the total to 73 unrelated cases.
quotes: In total, 19 of the 26 affected probands acquired the variant de novo, six acquired the variant with inheritance that was unknown because of a lack of parental genotype data and one case inherited variant n.76C>T from an affected mother.
We replicated this finding in three collections, bringing the number of unrelated cases to 73.

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) observed the RNU4-2 n.76C>T variant de novo in 4 families and inherited from an affected mother in 1 family. It was the only variant among the 74 pedigrees present in gnomAD (allele count 1 in 152,108). The authors suggested it may cause a less severe phenotype in some cases than other variants, particularly n.64_65insT. Variant n.76C>G was seen in 1 case without neurodevelopmental abnormality, further suggesting that some mutations at position 76 may have a limited or benign effect.
quotes: The n.76C>T variant is the only one among the 74 pedigrees that is present in gnomAD, where it has an allele count of one in 152,108.

the inheritance in one family and the observation in gnomAD suggest that it may cause a less severe phenotype in some cases than the other variants we identified, particularly the predominant variant n.64_65insT
variant n.76C>G was observed in one case without NDA, further suggesting that certain mutations at nucleotide position 76 may have a limited or benign effect

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) analyzed HPO terms for 46 RNU4-2 cases from the 100,000 Genomes Project coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality. Intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental delay were each present in 91% and motor delay in 61%. Compared with other cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality, several features were significantly overrepresented: microcephaly (57%), seizures (52%), generalized hypotonia (39%), proportionate short stature (28%), drooling (13%) and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion (13%).
quotes: Of these 46 cases, 91% had the ID term, 91% had ‘Neurodevelopmental delay’ and 61% had ‘Motor delay’, broadly in line with general term frequencies across ID cases

including ‘Microcephaly’ in 57% (versus 18% in other NDA-coded cases, Bonferroni-adjusted P = 3.23 × 10−7), ‘Drooling’ in 13% (versus 1%, P = 6.93 × 10−4), ‘Proportionate short stature’ in 28% (versus 7%, P = 7.60 × 10−4)
‘Generalized hypotonia’ in 39% (versus 13%, P = 8.08 × 10−4), ‘Seizure’ in 52% (versus 27%, P = 3.13 × 10−2) and ‘Abnormality of upper lip vermillion’ in 13% (versus 2%, P = 4.00 × 10−2)

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) found RNU4-2 cases in 46 of 9,112 (0.50%) 100,000 Genomes Project cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality, making it the most prevalent etiology for neurodevelopmental abnormality in that cohort. In the UK Genomic Medicine Service, RNU4-2 was the second most prevalent etiology (21 of 5,527 cases, 0.38%), after MECP2 (24 cases).
quotes: RNU4-2 was the most prevalent etiology for NDA in the 100KGP (Fig. 2b).
In the GMS, RNU4-2 was the second most prevalent etiology for NDA (21 of 5,527 NDA-coded cases, 0.38%) after MECP2 (24 cases)

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) reported that one variant region of RNU4-2 maps to the U4-U6 quasi-pseudoknot interaction and the other maps to U4-U6 stem III. They predicted that the variants destabilize U4 snRNA interactions with U6 snRNA and with RNA-binding proteins. Noting the similar phenotype of WBP4 deficiency, they suggested that delayed U4-U6 unwinding may be the underlying etiological mechanism.
quotes: one region maps to a quasi-pseudoknot interaction between U4 and U6 while the other maps to an interaction between U4 and U6 called stem III
a delay in U4–U6 unwinding activity similar to that observed in WBP4 deficiency might be the underlying etiological mechanism of this newly described syndrome

findings.statement: Greene et al. (2024) described a syndrome caused by de novo variants in 2 regions of RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 snRNA of the major spliceosome. The syndrome is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures and motor delay.
quotes: We implicated de novo variants among 47 cases in two regions of RNU4-2 in the etiology of a syndrome characterized by ID, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures and motor delay.
